name: Scalp advancement hairline lowering

card.summary: Surgery that removes a strip of forehead skin and advances the scalp forward, lowering a high hairline and shortening the forehead.
card.aka: Scalp advancement, hairline lowering, forehead reduction, scalp lifting
card.note: Surgical scar, temporary or permanent hair loss near the incision and numbness are documented; scalp laxity limits how far the hairline can move.

quick.overview:
Scalp advancement hairline lowering is a plastic-surgery procedure that moves the frontal hairline forward. A surgeon removes a band of forehead skin, frees the scalp from the skull and slides it forward, placing the incision so hair grows through the scar. For people with a naturally high hairline or a recessed one, it shortens a long forehead and changes facial proportions immediately.

How far the hairline can move depends mainly on how loose the scalp is. Tissue expanders can allow more advancement when laxity is limited. Hair transplants are the main alternative and add density rather than changing forehead height.
quick.how: The procedure is typically outpatient, under local anaesthesia with sedation or general anaesthesia. The surgeon marks a new hairline, often in a slightly irregular line to look natural, removes skin, undermines and advances the scalp, and closes in layers. It is often chosen by women and by people undergoing facial feminization, and may be combined with brow work or hair transplantation to camouflage the scar. Swelling and numbness settle over months.
quick.risks: Reported risks include a visible scar (which may show with cowlicks or later balding), temporary hair thinning called shock loss, permanent hair loss near the scar, persistent numbness, hematoma, infection and the possibility of revision. Older extensive scalp lifting and scalp reduction techniques carried risks of tissue death at the back of the scalp, which led surgeons to develop staged and delayed approaches.

lead: Hairline lowering, also called scalp advancement or forehead reduction, is surgery that moves the front hairline forward. It is used for a congenitally high hairline or one that has receded, and is performed mostly on women, with many facial feminization patients also having it to create a lower, more feminine hairline [1].

People use it to shorten a tall forehead and change facial thirds proportions in a single operation. Compared with follicular unit hair transplantation, which can take up to two years to reach comparable density, hairline lowering gives a near-immediate result [1].

The related older technique of extensive scalp lifting and scalp reduction was developed for male pattern baldness and has been described in surgical journals since the late 1980s; one author reported an eight-year experience of more than 1,230 cases [2]. Published studies on forehead hairline lowering itself are mainly small retrospective series and a pooled meta-analysis.

angle.text: The surgeon physically moves the scalp and hairline forward, so a high hairline sits lower right after surgery. People choose it to shorten the forehead and frame the face differently.

infobox: Local with IV sedation, or general [1]

paras: The surgeon marks the planned hairline, often as a wavy line, then removes excess forehead or scalp skin, separates the scalp from the skull and advances it. Incisions are placed so hair grows through the scar. Cutting the galea can give extra advancement, and sutures or implants may help hold the scalp. The wound is closed in two layers or with clips [1].

Scalp laxity is the main limit on how far the hairline can move. Tissue expanders can substantially increase possible advancement where laxity is insufficient [1]. Related older work described a horseshoe-shaped expander used with extensive scalp lifting in patients with very poor laxity [3].

Scalp flaps, in which a band of scalp with its blood supply is shifted over a bald area, date to the 19th century [4]. Extensive scalp lifting emerged in the 1980s for male pattern baldness and involved cutting both occipital arteries so the donor scalp could be undermined; surgeons reported necrosis at the nuchal ridge as a risk and developed ligation of the occipital arteries 4 to 8 weeks beforehand to reduce it [2][5]. Later work applied the same principles to circumferential scalp reduction [6]. Frontal hairline lowering is listed among modern hair-surgery applications for naturally high hairlines [4].

Published studies of forehead hairline lowering are mainly small retrospective series and a pooled meta-analysis; a systematic review and meta-analysis of forehead reduction outcomes exists in the literature.

In the older scalp-lifting literature, the author of an eight-year, 1,230-case series assessed necrosis, infection, hematoma, numbness and scarring and recommended occipital artery ligation 4 to 8 weeks before a scalp lift [2]. A study of occipital artery ligation as a priming step addressed the risk of necrosis [5]. A 2018 study of platelet-rich plasma with embedded sutures examined scalp lifting-related techniques in androgenetic alopecia [7].

Documented effects include a scar that is usually hidden by regrowth but can show with cowlicks or progressive balding, temporary shock loss, and rare infection; hair transplants can be used to cover the scar [1]. Older extensive scalp lifting carried a risk of necrosis at the nuchal ridge [5].
In communities focused on facial proportions, hairline lowering is discussed as a surgical option for a long forehead or high hairline, often compared with hair transplantation as an alternative.

timeline.event: Scalp flaps first used to cover bald areas [4].
Extensive scalp-lifting discussed in dermatologic surgery journals [2].
Occipital artery ligation described to reduce necrosis risk in scalp lifting [5].
